---
title: "Security and privacy"
---

Quartorium is meant to run on a server you control, for a research group and its
collaborators. This page describes what it protects against and what it doesn't.

## Links are keys

Collaborators don't have accounts. Each person gets a personal link with a random token
(18 random bytes, 144 bits), and the link is the only credential.

- Anyone who has a link can do what its owner can: read and edit the paper, comment, and,
  for a lead's link, accept suggestions, finish rounds and merge into main.
- Removing a person in **People** disables their link at once.
- Links survive into the next round. A finished round keeps a separate read-only link for
  the lead.
- Treat a lead's link like a password. Reviewers' links are less sensitive, because their
  edits are only suggestions and every action is recorded in Git under their name.

The admin pages (connecting repositories, starting rounds) are protected by
`QUARTORIUM_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and a signed, HTTP-only session cookie. Without a password, the
admin pages are disabled, but existing links keep working.

## Use HTTPS

Run Quartorium behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS (Caddy, nginx, Apache). Links and the admin
cookie are sent with every request, so plain HTTP would expose them on the network. See
[Getting started](getting-started.qmd#running-it-for-a-group).

## Code execution

Rendering runs `quarto render` on the paper, which **executes its code chunks** on the
server, with the server's permissions.

- **Collaborators can't add or change code.** Code chunks, raw blocks, HTML blocks and the
  YAML header are locked. The browser never sends them back: the server restores them from
  its own copy and rejects any save that adds, removes or reorders them. Typed text that
  looks like code (```` ```{r} ````, `<script>`, `{=html}`) is escaped by Pandoc and
  stays text. New citations are accepted only for known keys and are rebuilt by the server.
- **Code only comes from Git.** What is executed is what the repository's branches contain,
  that is, what someone with push access put there. Connect only repositories whose code you
  are willing to run on the server.
- Run the server as an unprivileged user (the example systemd unit does), ideally in a
  container or VM if the repository's contributors are not all trusted.
- Projects that use Quarto's `freeze` and commit `_freeze/` are rendered from the frozen
  results, so code doesn't need to run at all.
- Renders have a time limit (`QUARTORIUM_RENDER_TIMEOUT`, default 15 minutes).

## What is stored where

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| Your Git remote | the paper, comments, all decisions and history, with names (and e-mail addresses, if entered) as commit authors |
| `QUARTORIUM_DATA/quartorium.sqlite` | links, names, e-mail addresses, drafts not yet committed, which suggestions were decided, activity events, **Git access tokens** |
| `QUARTORIUM_DATA/repos/` | bare clones of the connected repositories |
| `QUARTORIUM_DATA/renders/` | rendered outputs and images |
| `QUARTORIUM_DATA/secret` | the key that signs the admin cookie (unless `QUARTORIUM_SECRET` is set) |

Keep the data folder readable only by the user running Quartorium, and back it up. The Git
access tokens are stored as entered, so use tokens that are limited to the paper's
repository and to reading and writing code (on Forgejo, Gitea and GitLab: a repository or
project access token).

Access tokens are never written into the clones' Git configuration or into commits. They are
passed to each Git command as an HTTP header and removed from error messages and from the
admin page.

## Personal data

- **Names** appear in the commit history as authors. Collaborators should know that the
  history is as permanent as the repository.
- **E-mail addresses** are optional. If entered, they are used for invitations and as the Git
  author e-mail. Without one, commits use a placeholder address.
- Quartorium has **no analytics, no tracking, no external requests** from the browser. Fonts,
  KaTeX and all scripts are served by Quartorium itself.
- Rendered pages can contain what your paper's code produces, including external resources
  if your code adds them.

## Reporting a problem

Please report security problems privately to the maintainer rather than in a public issue.
